cues.text: Chapter five looks at traditional and advanced database types.
The big question here is this: when you store data, what shape should that data take, and what does each shape cost you?
Let's walk through ten models, one at a time, and for each we will look at its structure, where it fits best, and its trade-off.
The first is the hierarchical model.
Its structure is a parent-child tree.
Every record sits under a parent, much like an organisation chart.
It is the best fit for strict organisational hierarchies, where each item clearly belongs to exactly one place.
The trade-off is that it has limited support for multiple-parent relationships.
If something naturally belongs under two parents, a tree struggles to represent it.
Second is the network model.
Here, records have multiple links.
So instead of a single parent, a record can connect to several others.
That makes it a good fit for complex navigational relationships, where you move from record to record following links.
The trade-off is complex access paths.
Because the links are so flexible, finding your way through them becomes complicated.
Third is the relational model.
Its structure is tables with keys and joins.
Rows live in tables, keys identify rows, and joins connect tables together.
It is the best fit for structured records and payments.
The trade-off is twofold: schema design, meaning you must plan the table structure carefully, and distributed scaling, meaning it takes more effort to spread across many machines.
Fourth is the object-oriented model.
Its structure is persistent objects and classes, so the objects your program works with are stored directly.
It suits complex engineering objects.
The trade-off is interoperability and tooling, meaning it can be harder to work with other systems, and the supporting tools are less widespread.
Fifth is the key-value model.
Its structure is simple: a key maps to a value.
You give the key, you get the value back.
It is the best fit for cache and session lookup.
The trade-off is limited ad hoc queries.
You are good at fetching by key, but not at asking flexible, unplanned questions.
Sixth is the document model.
Its structure is JSON-like documents.
It fits flexible product and telemetry records, where different records may have different fields.
The trade-off is duplication and consistency design.
Since related data may be copied into several documents, you must plan carefully to keep it consistent.
Seventh is the wide-column model.
Its structure is partitioned rows and column families.
It is the best fit for large distributed write workloads, where huge volumes of data are being written across many machines.
The trade-off is a query-driven schema.
That means you design your tables around the queries you plan to run, rather than around the data alone.
Eighth is the graph model.
Its structure is nodes, relationships, and properties.
Nodes are the things, relationships connect them, and properties describe both.
It is the best fit for fraud and network traversal, where you follow connections across many hops.
The trade-off is that it is less suitable for some aggregate workloads, such as summarising large amounts of data in bulk.
Ninth is NewSQL, also called distributed SQL.
Its structure is relational SQL with distributed transactions.
You keep the relational approach, but it runs across multiple machines.
It is the best fit for scalable transactional workloads.
The trade-off is coordination latency and complexity, because the machines must coordinate with each other, which takes time and adds difficulty.
Tenth is the time-series model.
Its structure is timestamp-oriented data, where time is the organising principle.
It is the best fit for sensor and monitoring data.
The trade-off is specialised query and storage patterns, meaning you must work in the ways this kind of store expects.
Now, some important clarifications, because these terms are often confused.
First, column-family NoSQL is not the same as an analytical column-oriented relational storage engine.
They both mention columns, but they are different things.
Second, NoSQL means "not only SQL." It does not imply no schema, no transactions, or no consistency.
Many people assume it does, and that assumption is wrong.
For example, MongoDB supports document validation and multi-document transactions, and you should use them when necessary.
Third, NewSQL seeks relational semantics and horizontal scalability.
It does not simply abandon ACID, the guarantees of reliable transactions.
Fourth, cloud and distributed are different ideas.
Cloud describes deployment and service delivery.
Distributed describes placement and coordination of data.
Both can coexist with several of the models we just covered.
Next, scaling.
Vertical scaling increases the capacity of one machine.
Horizontal scaling adds more machines.
Related to this, replication copies data, while sharding distributes different subsets of the data across machines.
Notice the difference: replication makes copies of the same data, while sharding splits the data into parts.
So how do you choose?
Base the decision on query patterns, integrity, latency, scale, operational skills, cost, security, and recovery requirements.
Finally, a hybrid or polyglot approach uses multiple stores, each for what it does best, but it introduces integration and governance costs.
More stores means more work to connect them and to manage them properly.
